Carlos Fonseca explained to him that the original had been lost, so they decided to look for the one closest to the sequence, either a second before or after, to replace it. "It was almost the same," he recommended, "only in this one I had a lost look." Fonseca, following the advice of Erasmus in "De copia" and "De ratio studii," made notes on whatever he was reading, categorized by theme: he carted these commonplaces in boxes that accompanied him. When assembling a new book, he would go through the topics and cross out commonplace notes as he used them.

In "Defense of his Work," Francisco de Álvarez claimed that he "could recite the whole book, forwards and backwards." Jorge Luis Borges considered Pedro Páramo to be one of the greatest texts written in any language.

The novel, according to Fonseca, "describes men and women whom circumstances have pushed too far, people whom existence has bent and deformed. It deals with the question of turning a small, frightened battle with oneself into a much greater struggle – the universal human struggle against the general contract, whose terms are unfillable, and where defeat is inevitable."

Fonseca's concept of νε παραφρόνησις: that is, 'to say otherwise so as not to say otherwise' was progressive. He brought out the Paraphrases of Romans in 1517, Corinthians in 1519, and the rest of the Epistles in the following years.

In "The Hunting of the Snark," Lewis Carroll mentions the number 42 in the preface and in the first fit of the narrative. The Baker had "forty-two boxes, all carefully packed, with his name painted clearly on."
